assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correcting spherical aberration turned the electron microscope into a routine sub-angstrom, atom-by-atom instrument for materials physics, chemistry and nanoscience. It is a clear invention that opened a door to phenomena people could not see before, and its impact is lasting and global.
assessment.attribution: The decisive path is fairly clean: Rose's theoretical design of the corrector, and Haider and Urban's first working realization in a TEM together with the demonstration of the resolution gain. The three credited names map onto that chain. Other groups (for example in scanning TEM) developed parallel correctors, and I have not independently verified who is owed credit there.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly mature: decades of commercial instruments, independent confirmation and widespread use. Recognition is, if anything, overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Credit for the STEM-side corrector (Krivanek and collaborators) is outside the supplied names and could be contested.
Whether the committee regards this as physics rather than a methods contribution that belongs in another prize field.
As a microscopist I should be alert to my own proximity to this field when weighing it against other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental observation of the Higgs boson completed the Standard Model and verified a prediction half a century old. It is the original experimental discovery of a new particle, with very high importance for our understanding of nature, and it is unrecognized on the experimental side after the 2013 prize for the theory.
assessment.attribution: This is the hardest part. The discovery was a collaboration of thousands, and the supplied names are four founders and leaders of ATLAS and CMS. Only three can be named, so one must be left out. I propose Gianotti (ATLAS spokesperson at the time of announcement), Jenni (ATLAS founding spokesperson) and Della Negra (CMS co-founder). Virdee has an equally strong claim on the CMS side, so this choice is a judgement, not a clear result of the record. Whether leaders rather than a collaboration can fairly be honoured is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Mature: the 2012 observation has been confirmed by two independent experiments and by extensive coupling measurements since. The timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Fair allocation among four credited leaders with only three places; the CMS side may be under-represented.
Whether leadership roles correspond to 'the people doing the original work' in the sense the committee requires.
Possible view that the 2013 prize for the theory already covers the principal recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and brought by Ye's group to the 10^-18 fractional uncertainty level, opened the door to precision tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a future redefinition of the second. This is a tool that lets us see effects that could not be measured before.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations; Ye's group pushed the performance to the limit and showed the many-body, spin-resolved clock. Two names support a clean prize configuration. Hall and Hänsch were honoured in 2005 for the comb technology that underlies the readout, so there is some overlap with an earlier prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense that several independent labs have reproduced and surpassed the original results. The redefinition of the SI second is still pending, so societal impact is slightly early, though the science is secure.
uncertainties: Contributions of other groups to lattice-clock development (for example ion clocks and other Sr clock laboratories) may deserve credit.
Degree of overlap with the 2005 prize for frequency combs.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new class of electronic phases, and the experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells is a clear, original experiment confirming a surprising prediction. The concept has had lasting influence far beyond the original system.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state in graphene; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental observation in HgTe wells (2007), following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The supplied credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and also the three-dimensional topological insulator work, so credit for the compound discovery is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent experimental confirmation in several material systems, and the interpretation has been stable for more than a decade. Recognition is timely or somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe proposal (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is not in the supplied names.
The three-dimensional topological insulator discoveries are a separate part of the story that may need separate recognition.
Kane and Mele's graphene prediction is not itself the realized system.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at magic angles and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened a very productive field of tunable quantum matter. It is an original experiment that, together with the preceding theory, changed how people engineer electronic phases.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald supplied the theoretical flat-band prediction (2011) and Jarillo-Herrero's group the 2018 experimental observation. The experiment was carried out by a team including first author Yuan Cao, who is not among the supplied names, so the decisive experimental contribution beyond the group leader is not fully represented. Three names are a fair configuration only if the committee accepts group-leader credit.
assessment.maturity: Relatively young (about eight years) but replicated by many groups, with a stable interpretation of the single-particle flat bands. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so full maturity is not yet reached.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity remains contested.
Credit to junior experimentalists such as Yuan Cao and to other earlier theory contributors is outside the supplied names.
Possible prematurity relative to older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy spins in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state quantum system and made nanoscale quantum sensing possible, including for biology and materials. It is an instrument-type breakthrough that lets us see magnetic and electric fields on scales previously inaccessible.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group was central to the first optical detection of single NV centres (1997), and Jelezko and Wrachtrup demonstrated coherent control in 2004. I propose the two experimentalists and leave out Lukin, whose contribution was largely theory and later quantum-network and sensing extensions, so that the prize follows the original experiments. This choice is a judgement.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the basic science and widely replicated; applications in quantum sensing are still developing, so the practical impact is partly forward-looking.
uncertainties: Credit for early NV work by other groups is not in the supplied names.
Whether quantum sensing applications are mature enough to demonstrate benefit.
Lukin's exclusion may be disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube detected a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and later associated neutrinos with the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane, opening neutrino astronomy as a new window on the sky. This is an original, verified discovery built on an unusual instrument, a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube and Karle was a central figure in its construction and the discovery analysis, but the discovery is the result of a large collaboration. Two names are a feasible prize configuration, but the contributions of the AMANDA pioneers and other IceCube leaders are unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by independent analyses and multi-messenger follow-up, though identification of individual sources is still developing. It is mature enough for the discovery of a diffuse flux, with recognition becoming timely.
uncertainties: Source identification remains incomplete, and the TXS 0506+056 association has modest significance.
Large-collaboration attribution and the role of pioneers in the DUMAND and AMANDA projects.
Parallel work by other neutrino telescopes may matter for a fair record.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1992 discovery of the first Kuiper Belt object beyond Neptune confirmed a population of icy bodies in the outer Solar System and changed our understanding of planetary formation and the status of Pluto. It is a clear original observational discovery that is easy to state and important for planetary physics.
assessment.attribution: Jewitt and Luu together found 1992 QB1 after a multi-year survey, and the credit is direct and cleanly shared between two people. Earlier theoretical predictions of such a belt are not covered by the supplied names. The prize would also recognise a woman who did the original work, which I welcome, but I do not let that decide the ranking.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: many hundreds of objects were found subsequently, and the interpretation is stable. The recognition is long overdue, so the question is mainly whether the committee treats it as physics.
uncertainties: Whether the committee considers the subject to fall within physics rather than astronomy-led planetary science.
Predecessor theoretical work and other early survey claims that might lead to disputes over originality.
